name: Zephaniah
author: Zephaniah was a prophet, someone who spoke messages he believed came from God, and he seems to have lived in or near Jerusalem. The book's opening line traces his family back four generations to a man named Hezekiah, possibly the well-known King Hezekiah, which would make Zephaniah a distant relative of the royal family, though this is not certain. Beyond this family line, almost nothing is known about his life.
audience: His first hearers were the people of Judah, the small southern kingdom of the Israelites, and especially the residents of its capital, Jerusalem. Many had drifted into worshipping other gods alongside the God of Israel, and the leaders and wealthy classes were comfortable and confident.
era: The book places Zephaniah in the reign of King Josiah, who ruled Judah from about 640 to 609 BC, and many think he spoke before Josiah's major religious reforms began around 622 BC. Before Josiah, King Manasseh's long reign had filled Judah with the worship of foreign gods. The great empire of Assyria, which had dominated the region for a century, was weakening, and Babylon was rising; Assyria's capital, Nineveh, fell in 612 BC.

notes.1:2: The practices named here, Baal worship, bowing to the stars on rooftops and honouring the god Milcom, flourished under Manasseh and were later removed by Josiah.
notes.1:7: The Fish Gate, the Second Quarter and the Mortar were real districts of Jerusalem, the last probably a hollow where merchants and traders did business.
notes.2:4: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron were Philistine cities on the coastal plain west of Judah, long-standing rivals of the Israelites.
notes.2:8: Moab and Ammon were neighbouring peoples east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea, with a long history of hostility toward Israel and Judah.
notes.2:12: Cush was the land along the upper Nile, south of Egypt; Assyria's capital Nineveh was the greatest city of the day, destroyed by Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.
notes.3:14: Traditionally this closing song is read as Zephaniah's own; some scholars think it was added later, perhaps after the exile to Babylon.

flags.problem: Wrong anchor. Baal worship, bowing to the stars on rooftops and Milcom are named in 1:4–5, not 1:2. Readers who open 1:2 will see a note that doesn't match their verse. Milcom is also not identified, and an ordinary reader won't know who he was.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 1:4 and identify Milcom briefly, e.g. 'the god Milcom, worshipped by the neighbouring Ammonites'.

flags.problem: Wrong anchor. The Fish Gate, the Second Quarter and the Mortar appear in 1:10–11, not 1:7. The note also calls all three 'districts', but the Fish Gate was a city gate.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 1:10 and reword, e.g. 'The Fish Gate was one of Jerusalem's city gates; the Second Quarter and the Mortar were districts of the city, the last probably a hollow where merchants and traders did business.'

flags.problem: States as fact that Josiah's major reforms began around 622 BC. That is the date in 2 Kings, tied to finding the law scroll in the temple. 2 Chronicles says his purge of foreign worship began earlier, around 628 BC, so the start date is not settled.
flags.suggestion: Hedge or broaden it, e.g. 'before Josiah's major religious reforms, which reached their height around 622 BC'.
